content: 1. Tucatinib can increase the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by interfering with the metabolism of the hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. It is recommended to avoid using these drugs together or consider alternative medications. If concurrent use is unavoidable, the dose of the CYP3A substrate should be reduced as per product labeling, and close monitoring is essential. Ethinyl estradiol may reduce the effectiveness of ursodiol due to pharmacodynamic antagonism, so caution and close monitoring are advised. 2. Vadadustat can increase the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol through mechanisms not fully understood. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 3. Ethinyl estradiol and valoctocogene roxaparvovec may both increase certain effects (mechanism unspecified). Caution and close monitoring are advised. Medications that can cause hepatotoxicity, when combined with valoctocogene roxaparvovec, may elevate the risk of liver enzyme abnormalities. These medications should be closely monitored, and alternative treatments should be considered if drug interactions are likely. 4. Ethinyl estradiol can decrease the levels or effects of valproic acid by increasing its elimination, potentially leading to an increased frequency of seizures. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. 5. Verapamil can increase the levels or effects of etonogestrel by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. Similarly, voriconazole can increase the levels or effects of both etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol by interfering with CYP3A4 metabolism. Zafirlukast also increases the levels or effects of etonogestrel through the same mechanism. In all cases, caution and close monitoring are necessary. 6. Reported side effects of hormonal contraceptives include decreased libido, hypersensitivity reactions (such as anaphylaxis and angioedema), stroke, arterial thromboembolic events (e.g., myocardial infarction), and exacerbation of varicose veins. Skin-related issues include urticaria, chloasma, and hereditary or acquired angioedema. Reproductive system disorders include penile reactions in male partners of NuvaRing users, galactorrhea, and vaginal injuries associated with ring breakage. 7. Documented contraindications for combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs) include arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction), thromboembolic disorders (e.g., DVT/PE), estrogen-dependent neoplasia, cerebrovascular or coronary artery disease, severe liver disease, undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding, uncontrolled hypertension, and a history of breast cancer. Women over 35 who smoke, those with diabetes mellitus with vascular involvement, or those undergoing major surgery with prolonged immobilization should avoid CHCs. 8. CHCs may exacerbate conditions such as depression, endometriosis, diabetes, hypertension, renal or hepatic impairment, and diseases worsened by fluid retention (e.g., migraines, asthma, epilepsy). Women with risk factors for venous thromboembolism (VTE), such as smoking, obesity, or a family history of VTE, should avoid CHCs. The risk of VTE is highest during the first year of CHC use and after restarting following a break of at least four weeks. 9. Estrogens may cause retinal vascular thrombosis, so therapy should be stopped if visual disturbances arise. Women with hypertriglyceridemia or a family history of it may be at increased risk of pancreatitis when using CHCs. 10. CHCs may affect lipid profiles and serum triglycerides, potentially worsening gallbladder disease or causing adverse lipid changes in some women. Women with a history of CHC-related cholestasis or pregnancy-related cholestasis are at increased risk of recurrence. 11. Extensive studies have shown no increased risk of birth defects in women who used oral contraceptives before pregnancy. However, oral contraceptives should not be used during pregnancy or to treat threatened or habitual abortion. If pregnancy is confirmed, oral contraceptive use should be discontinued. 12. Small amounts of oral contraceptive steroids have been detected in the milk of nursing mothers, with some reported adverse effects on infants, such as jaundice and breast enlargement. Oral contraceptives may also interfere with lactation by reducing the quantity and quality of breast milk. Nursing mothers should be advised to use alternative contraception until they have completely weaned their child. 13. The NuvaRing is inserted into the vagina and remains in place for three weeks, followed by a one-week break during which withdrawal bleeding typically occurs. A new ring is then inserted after the one-week break. Women should adhere to the recommended regimen to maintain contraceptive efficacy. 14. Cases of toxic shock syndrome (TSS) have been reported in NuvaRing users, though a causal relationship has not been established. If TSS is suspected, appropriate medical evaluation and treatment should be initiated. 15. Women with liver disease, such as acute viral hepatitis or severe cirrhosis, should not use CHCs. Acute or chronic liver function disturbances may necessitate discontinuation of CHCs until liver function markers normalize. 16. 17. Hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis and angioedema, have been reported. If these occur, CHC use should be discontinued, and appropriate treatment should be administered. 18. Women with diabetes or prediabetes should be carefully monitored while using CHCs, as these may decrease glucose tolerance. Alternative contraception should be considered for women with uncontrolled dyslipidemia. 19. The CDC recommends waiting at least four weeks after vaginal birth or six weeks after cesarean section before initiating CHCs in non-breastfeeding women to reduce the risk of VTE. Women with additional VTE risk factors should avoid CHCs altogether. 20. The risk of postpartum thromboembolism decreases after the third postpartum week, while the risk of ovulation increases. 21. The NuvaRing may not be suitable for women with conditions that make the vagina more susceptible to irritation or ulceration. Cases of vaginal or cervical erosion or ulceration have been reported, with some requiring removal by a healthcare provider. 22. Adding plans allows for comparison of formulary status with other drugs in the same class. Formulary information may vary and change over time, so it is essential to contact the applicable plan provider for the most current details.
